c.tagline: Black Sea port of misty monasteries, tea and hazelnut hills.

taxi.fareNote: Taxis are yellow and metered; Uber in Turkey dispatches licensed taxis, and the BiTaksi and iTaksi apps are the easiest way to hail one and pay a fair fare.

emergency.note: 112 is now Turkey's single emergency number for police, ambulance and fire.

hood_desc: The city's central square and social hub, a tree-shaded plaza ringed by hotels, cafes, teahouses and the main shopping streets; the obvious walkable base for first-timers, close to everything.

The historic old town on the ridge between two ravines, where the Byzantine-era Ortahisar (Fatih) Mosque, the castle walls and steep stone lanes recall Trabzon's Trebizond past; best for sightseeing and history.
A busy central district just off Meydan packed with restaurants, meyhanes, patisseries and the Uzun Sokak shopping street; the go-to area for dining and going out.
A green hilltop above the city crowned by the Boztepe park and tea gardens with sweeping views over Trabzon and the Black Sea; a calm, largely residential area popular for sunset.

water.note: Officially treated but most visitors and many locals drink bottled water.

transit.hours: City buses and dolmuş minibuses run from around 6:00 AM to midnight; dolmuşes leave when full and cover the late-evening gaps.
transit.note: Trabzon has no metro or tram; the hilly city runs on municipal buses and a dense web of dolmuş minibuses, backed up by taxis and app-based taxi hailing.
transit.pay: City buses use the rechargeable TrabzonKart smartcard, tapped on boarding; dolmuşes are paid in cash to the driver. Fares are in Turkish lira.

bus: Intercity coaches from Trabzon Otogar (Metro Turizm, Ulusoy and others)
ferry: Trabzon Port (cargo and occasional seasonal passenger services)

transit.m: Havalimanı dolmuş / city bus to Meydan (Atatürk Alanı) (~20-30 min)
Taxi to the city center (~10-15 min)

tip.r: Not obligatory; rounding up the bill or leaving about 5-10% for good restaurant service is customary.

food.name: Hamsi tava
food.desc: Black Sea anchovies rolled in cornmeal and fried in a pan until crisp, eaten whole with raw onion, lemon and cornbread. Best from November to February.

places.name: Balikcilar Carsisi (Faroz fish market)
places.note: Buy hamsi off the boats at the harbour and the market cooks fry it for you.

places.name: Baliklama Balik Lokantasi
places.note: Pick your fish from the ice and it is cooked to order minutes later.

places.name: Ganita seafront restaurants
places.note: Row of fish houses on the coastal park, popular with families in hamsi season.

food.name: Akcaabat koftesi
food.desc: Trabzon's famous meatball: hand-minced veal with garlic and a little bread, grilled over charcoal so it stays juicy and faintly smoky.

places.name: Cemilusta
places.note: The best-known name in town for Akcaabat kofte, with sides and fresh bread.

places.name: Kamiloglu Kofte
places.note: Tucked under the stairs near the market; locals also buy the kofte by the kilo.

places.name: Niyaz Usta
places.note: In the town that gave the kofte its name, a short drive west of Trabzon.

food.name: Kuymak (muhlama)
food.desc: Molten cornmeal beaten with butter and stringy Trabzon cheese until it pulls in ropes. Eaten straight from the copper pan at breakfast.

places.name: Vosporos Cafe
places.note: Serves a famously stringy kuymak in a quiet private courtyard.

places.name: Uzun Sokak breakfast salons
places.note: The city's main pedestrian street is lined with kahvalti places doing pan-to-table kuymak.

places.name: Ganita seafront cafes
places.note: Sea-view weekend breakfast spreads with kuymak at the centre of the table.

food.name: Vakfikebir bread
food.desc: A giant sourdough loaf baked in a wood-fired stone oven, sold by weight. Thick crust, dense crumb, and it keeps for days without going stale.

places.name: Vakfikebir village bakeries
places.note: The only place the loaf is still made to the original wood-oven method.

places.name: Taskin Vakfikebir Ekmek Firini
places.note: City branch of the Vakfikebir tradition; loaves come out through the day.

places.name: Uzun Sokak bakeries
places.note: Central bakeries sell half and quarter loaves if a whole one is too much.

food.name: Karalahana
food.desc: Black Sea collard greens, cooked either as a thick soup with beans and cornmeal or rolled around rice and minced meat as sarma.

places.name: Uzun Sokak lokantas
places.note: Home-style steam-table canteens where the daily pots always include karalahana.

places.name: Cemilusta
places.note: Keeps regional vegetable dishes on the menu alongside the grill.

places.name: Ganita seafront restaurants
places.note: Order it as a warm starter before the fish; very much a local order.

food.name: Hamsikoy sutlaci
food.desc: Rice pudding from the mountain village of Hamsikoy, made with local milk and blistered under a grill until the top is scorched brown.

places.name: Hamsikoy village pudding houses
places.note: Worth the mountain drive; several cafes have made it here for generations.

places.name: Hamsikoy Sutlaci shops
places.note: City-centre branches sell the same pudding in clay dishes if you cannot get up the pass.

places.name: Meydan Park cafes
places.note: Central square cafes serve it warm with tea in the evening.

food.name: Black Sea tea
food.desc: Almost all Turkish tea is grown on the hillsides just east of here. It is poured strong from a double pot into tulip glasses, all day, everywhere.

places.name: Meydan Park tea gardens
places.note: Trabzon's central square is ringed with shaded tea gardens; the default meeting place.

places.name: Boztepe hilltop tea gardens
places.note: Tea with the whole city and the Black Sea laid out below; go at sunset.

places.name: Ganita seafront tea houses
places.note: Glasses of tea at the water's edge, with the fishing boats coming in.

food.name: Ayran
food.desc: Salted, whipped yoghurt drink served frothy and ice-cold. In Trabzon it is the standard partner to charcoal-grilled kofte.

places.name: Cemilusta
places.note: Churned ayran poured from a copper jug, exactly what the kofte needs.

places.name: Kamiloglu Kofte
places.note: Cheap, foamy, and served in a metal cup alongside the meatballs.

places.name: Uzun Sokak lokantas
places.note: Every canteen on the street has an ayran churn spinning by the till.

landmarks: Hagia Sophia of Trabzon (Ayasofya Mosque)
A 13th-century church of the Empire of Trebizond, adorned with remarkable Byzantine frescoes and stone friezes, set in gardens overlooking the sea.
Atatürk Pavilion (Atatürk Köşkü)
A gleaming white 1903 mansion in pine-forested hills above the city, gifted to Atatürk, preserves elegant period interiors and manicured flower gardens.
Boztepe Hill
Trabzon's favourite panoramic terrace, where tea gardens overlook the sprawling city and harbour, perfect at dusk with a glass of Rize tea.
Trabzon Castle Walls
Byzantine ramparts from the city's days as imperial Trebizond climb from the shore through the old town, dividing districts above dramatic ravines.
Trabzon Museum (Kostaki Mansion)
A banker's opulent early-1900s mansion showcases stuccoed ceilings and archaeology, including a striking bronze statue of Hermes unearthed nearby.
Gülbahar Hatun Mosque
Built in 1514 by Sultan Selim I for his mother, this graceful early-Ottoman mosque and tomb honour Trabzon's beloved princess-benefactress.
Meydan Square (Atatürk Alanı)
The city's social heart brims with tea houses, statues and pide restaurants, the starting point for exploring bazaars sloping toward the harbour.
Sera Lake (Sera Gölü)
A landslide-formed lake in a green valley just west of Trabzon, ringed by walking paths and lakeside fish restaurants popular on weekends.
Bedesten Bazaar
A domed 16th-century covered market near the city center where artisans sell silver jewelry, textiles, and handcrafted souvenirs beneath vaulted stone arches.
Fatih Mosque (Chrysokephalos)
A former Byzantine cathedral converted to a mosque after the 1461 Ottoman conquest, its interior still hiding Roman-era mosaics beneath carpet and glass flooring.

train.note: Trabzon has no railway - the eastern Black Sea coast was never connected, and the long-discussed line remains unbuilt. The nearest stations are at Erzurum and Sivas, both a long drive south across the mountains. Arrive by coach or fly into Trabzon airport.

intl.to: Batumi & Tbilisi (Georgia) - via the Sarp border

intl.op: Lüks Karadeniz — tickets at the Trabzon otogar

bus.note: Trabzon is the main overland gateway to Georgia: coaches run east along the coast to the Sarp border and on to Batumi in about 4 hours and Tbilisi in 10-12. Carry your passport; most nationalities do not need a Georgian visa but check first. Domestic coaches from the otogar reach Rize, Erzurum, Ankara and Istanbul (about 17 hours), bookable through obilet (https://www.obilet.com/en/).

ferry.note: There is no reliable scheduled passenger ferry from Trabzon. Black Sea sailings to Sochi in Russia have run on and off over the years and are not dependable for 2026 - check locally at the port before planning around one. Trabzon's harbour is otherwise a cargo and fishing port.

full.blurb: A cloud-wrapped plateau of tea gardens, hot springs and alpine pastures in the Kaçkar Mountains, about 2.5-3 hours east.
full.name: Ayder Yaylası (Rize highlands)

full.blurb: The heart of Turkey's tea country, with hillside plantations, the Ziraat botanical tea garden and Firtina valley beyond (~1.5-2h).
full.name: Rize

full.blurb: A dramatic mountain pass and old silver-mining region on the road inland, with the Karaca Cave and highland scenery (~1.5-2h).
full.name: Zigana & Gümüşhane

half.blurb: A spectacular Greek Orthodox monastery clinging to a sheer cliff in the forested Altındere valley near Maçka, about an hour south.
half.name: Sumela Monastery

half.blurb: A postcard mountain lake ringed by mist, mosques and wooden chalets in the highlands, about 1.5 hours southeast.
half.name: Uzungöl

half.blurb: A coastal town west of the city famous for its köfte meatballs and an old Ortamahalle quarter of timber houses (~30 min).
half.name: Akçaabat
